author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: The year 1775 was full of extreme opposites. On one hand, it was a time of great hope, wisdom, and light. On the other hand, it was a time of terrible despair, foolishness, and darkness. Everything seemed to be at its absolute best and its absolute worst at the exact same time, marking it as a very confusing period in history.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: The king and queen of England, and the king and queen of France, all believed their societies were perfectly ordered. They were completely convinced that their rule would last forever without any problems, and that the regular people would always be kept in their place.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: People in England at this time were strangely obsessed with minor superstitions and ghosts. They spent a lot of time talking about these trivial domestic ghost stories, while completely ignoring the incredibly important political messages and events that were arriving from America.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: France was violently oppressive to its citizens. The state brutally tortured people for minor offenses, completely unaware of the revolution that was coming. While the French authorities were spending money recklessly, the forces of Fate and Death were silently preparing the tools that would soon be used in the revolution.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: England was incredibly dangerous and lawless. Robberies were common every single night in London. The legal system was completely ineffective at stopping crime, so it relied heavily on the death penalty for even small crimes, constantly executing people without making the streets any safer.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: Despite all these massive problems and the obvious signs of coming disaster, the rulers continued to act with total authority. They blindly guided their countries through the year 1775, completely unaware of the historical forces working against them.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: On a Friday night in late November, the Dover mail coach was slowly climbing a muddy hill. The passengers had gotten out of the coach and were walking beside it because the horses were struggling so much to pull it up the steep, muddy slope.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: The horses were completely exhausted and struggling through the thick mud. They constantly stopped and stumbled, acting as if they were going to collapse from the effort of pulling the heavy coach.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: A thick, intensely cold fog covered the hill, rolling in like waves. It made it impossible for the passengers or the coach driver to see very far ahead, creating a very spooky and isolated atmosphere around the struggling coach.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_plain_text: The passengers were completely bundled up in heavy coats and boots against the cold. They deeply distrusted each other and the people they met on the road, because highway robberies were so common that anyone could secretly be a criminal.
